items.stem: Which term describes the following? The thought or belief aspect of an attitude about the attitude object.
items.answer: cognitive component
items.markingKey: (b) cognitive component: the thought or belief aspect of an attitude about the attitude object.
options: actor-observer effect
cognitive component
balance theory
cognitive dissonance

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes is NOT correct?
items.answer: Valence tells how central an attitude is.
items.markingKey: (d) It is incorrect. Valence tells whether the attitude is positive or negative.
options: Attitudes have affective, cognitive and behavioural components.
The four features of attitudes are valence, extremeness, simplicity or complexity, and centrality.
Attitudes are relatively stable and have an evaluative feature.
Valence tells how central an attitude is.

items.stem: Give a reason for the following: Attitudes are evaluative.
items.answer: They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object. (1 mark for the reason, 1 for linking it to the statement).

items.stem: The following statement about explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and justify your correction: "Attitudes are momentary and change every day."
items.answer: Attitudes are relatively stable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement (Attitudes are relatively stable.); 1 mark for a supporting fact from the NCERT chapter.

items.stem:
Read the following statements about explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes:
I. Attitudes are momentary and change every day.
II. Attitudes are relatively stable and have an evaluative feature.
III. The four features of attitudes are valence, extremeness, simplicity or complexity, and centrality.
Which of these statements are correct?
items.answer: II and III only
items.markingKey: (a) I is incorrect: Attitudes are relatively stable. II is correct. III is correct.
options: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I only

items.stem: Read the case and answer. Raju strongly dislikes cricket and refuses to watch even a single match. Name the features of attitude shown here and explain it briefly.
items.answer: Negative valence and high extremeness: valence tells that the attitude is negative; extremeness tells how strongly negative it is.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming it (negative valence and high extremeness); 1 mark for the explanation (valence tells that the attitude is negative; extremeness tells how strongly negative it is).

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"An attitude system may include several related attitudes about one object. Attitudes have affective, cognitive and behavioural components. Attitudes are relatively stable and have an evaluative feature. The four features of attitudes are valence, extremeness, simplicity or complexity, and centrality."
(i) Explain the term 'cognitive component', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: Attitudes are evaluative. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "An attitude has only an emotional component." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) The thought or belief aspect of an attitude about the attitude object. (ii) They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: It has affective, cognitive and behavioural components.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) The thought or belief aspect of an attitude about the attitude object. (ii) They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: It has affective, cognitive and behavioural components.

items.stem: Explain the four features of attitudes.
items.answer: Valence – positive or negative; extremeness – how positive or negative; simplicity or complexity – number of attitudes within the attitude system; centrality – role of the attitude in the system.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: Valence – positive or negative; extremeness – how positive or negative; simplicity or complexity – number of attitudes within the attitude system; centrality – role of the attitude in the system.

items.stem:
Statement: An attitude with high centrality is hard to change.
Which one of the following best explains this statement?
items.answer: It influences many other attitudes in the attitude system.
items.markingKey: (b) It influences many other attitudes in the attitude system.
options: They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object.
It influences many other attitudes in the attitude system.
They contain a behavioural component, a tendency to act in a certain way.
Ingroup bias makes people look down upon the outgroup.

items.stem: Which term describes the following? A group whose norms an individual accepts as a model for attitudes and behaviour.
items.answer: reference group
items.markingKey: (b) reference group: a group whose norms an individual accepts as a model for attitudes and behaviour.
options: ingroup bias
reference group
attitude
cognitive dissonance

items.stem:
Consider the following statements about attitude formation and change:
I. Family, school, reference groups, personal experiences and the media are factors in attitude formation.
II. In Heider's theory, balance exists when the P-O-X triangle has three positive sides or two negative and one positive side.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
items.answer: Both I and II
items.markingKey: (c) I is correct. II is correct.
options: I only
II only
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about attitude formation and change is correct?
items.answer: According to Festinger, the cognitive components of an attitude must be consonant.
items.markingKey: (a) The others are wrong: Three positive sides produce balance. Attitudes are learnt through experience, association, modelling and group norms. It was given by Fritz Heider; Festinger gave cognitive dissonance.
options: According to Festinger, the cognitive components of an attitude must be consonant.
Attitudes are inherited and cannot be learnt.
In the P-O-X triangle three positive sides produce imbalance.
Balance theory was given by Leon Festinger.

items.stem:
Statement: Children often share their parents' attitudes.
Which one of the following best explains this statement?
items.answer: Attitudes are learnt in the family through association, reward and modelling.
items.markingKey: (b) Attitudes are learnt in the family through association, reward and modelling.
options: The fundamental attribution error gives more weight to internal factors for others' behaviour.
Attitudes are learnt in the family through association, reward and modelling.
A highly credible source makes the message more convincing to the target.
The two cognitions are dissonant and the person reduces dissonance by changing one of them.

items.stem: Explain the two-step concept of attitude change.
items.answer: Proposed by S.M. Mohsin; step 1 – the target identifies with the source (liking, respect); step 2 – the source shows attitude change, and the target imitates it; the source should be credible.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: Proposed by S.M. Mohsin; step 1 – the target identifies with the source (liking, respect); step 2 – the source shows attitude change, and the target imitates it; the source should be credible.

items.stem:
Match List I with List II and choose the correct option.
List I:
A. Fritz Heider
B. Solomon Asch
C. Leon Festinger
D. S.M. Mohsin
List II:
1. conformity and impression formation
2. two-step concept
3. cognitive dissonance
4. balance theory
items.markingKey: (a) Fritz Heider – balance theory; Solomon Asch – conformity and impression formation; Leon Festinger – cognitive dissonance; S.M. Mohsin – two-step concept.

items.stem: "Attitudes are easier to change when the source is credible." Examine this statement with reference to attitude formation and change.
items.answer: The statement is valid. A highly credible source makes the message more convincing to the target.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: 1 for accepting or qualifying the statement, 1 for the reason (a highly credible source makes the message more convincing to the target.), 1 for supporting evidence from the chapter.

items.stem: Explain any four factors that influence attitude change.
items.answer: Characteristics of the existing attitude – valence, extremeness, centrality; source – credibility, attractiveness; message – rational or emotional appeal, motives activated; target – persuasibility, prejudice, self-esteem, intelligence.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: Characteristics of the existing attitude – valence, extremeness, centrality; source – credibility, attractiveness; message – rational or emotional appeal, motives activated; target – persuasibility, prejudice, self-esteem, intelligence.

items.stem: Distinguish between balance and imbalance in the P-O-X triangle.
items.answer: Balance – all three sides positive, or two negative and one positive; imbalance – all three negative, or two positive and one negative; imbalance leads to attitude change.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: Balance – all three sides positive, or two negative and one positive; imbalance – all three negative, or two positive and one negative; imbalance leads to attitude change.

items.stem: What is meant by 'cognitive dissonance' in the context of attitude formation and change?
items.answer: Leon Festinger's idea that inconsistency between two cognitions produces discomfort that leads to attitude change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cognitive dissonance correctly explained as Leon Festinger's idea that inconsistency between two cognitions produces discomfort that leads to attitude change.

items.stem: Give a reason for the following: A smoker who knows smoking causes cancer may stop smoking.
items.answer: The two cognitions are dissonant and the person reduces dissonance by changing one of them.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: The two cognitions are dissonant and the person reduces dissonance by changing one of them. (1 mark for the reason, 1 for linking it to the statement).

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about attitude formation and change is NOT correct?
items.answer: Attitudes are inherited and cannot be learnt.
items.markingKey: (a) It is incorrect. Attitudes are learnt through experience, association, modelling and group norms.
options: Attitudes are inherited and cannot be learnt.
Attitudes are learnt through association, reward and punishment, modelling, group norms and exposure to information.
In Mohsin's two-step concept, the target first identifies with the source and the source then shows attitude change.
Characteristics of the existing attitude, the source and the message, and the target all affect attitude change.

items.stem: Which of these is a strategy for handling prejudice?
items.answer: Intergroup contact
items.markingKey: (c) Intergroup contact.
options: Reducing education
Strengthening ingroup bias
Intergroup contact

items.stem:
Consider the following statements about attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination:

items.answer: Both I and II
items.markingKey: (c) I is correct. II is correct.
options: I only
II only
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination is correct?
items.answer: Education, intergroup contact, highlighting individual identity and minimising learning of prejudice are strategies to handle prejudice.
items.markingKey: (b) The others are wrong: Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is the behaviour. Stereotypes overgeneralise and ignore individual differences. Attitudes predict behaviour only under certain conditions, as LaPiere's study showed.
options: Prejudice and discrimination are the same thing.
Education, intergroup contact, highlighting individual identity and minimising learning of prejudice are strategies to handle prejudice.
Attitudes always predict behaviour.
Stereotypes are accurate descriptions of every member of a group.

items.stem:
Statement: Members of a group may confirm the prejudice about them.
Which one of the following best explains this statement?
items.answer: The self-fulfilling prophecy makes them behave as others expect.
items.markingKey: (a) The self-fulfilling prophecy makes them behave as others expect.
options: The self-fulfilling prophecy makes them behave as others expect.
It brings the groups together in a cooperative setting and corrects stereotypes.
Ingroup bias makes people look down upon the outgroup.
The fundamental attribution error gives more weight to internal factors for others' behaviour.

items.stem: Describe any three sources of prejudice.
items.answer: Learning – from family, reference groups, media; strong social identity and ingroup bias; scapegoating – blaming a weaker group; kernel of truth; self-fulfilling prophecy.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: Learning – from family, reference groups, media; strong social identity and ingroup bias; scapegoating – blaming a weaker group; kernel of truth; self-fulfilling prophecy.

items.stem: Read the case and answer. Students told repeatedly that their group is 'bad at studies' stop trying and begin to score poorly. Name the source of prejudice shown here and explain it briefly.
items.answer: Self-fulfilling prophecy: the target of prejudice behaves in a way that confirms the negative belief.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming it (self-fulfilling prophecy); 1 mark for the explanation (the target of prejudice behaves in a way that confirms the negative belief).

items.stem: In the study of attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination, the term 'discrimination' refers to:
items.answer: The behavioural component of prejudice, shown as unfair treatment of members of a group
items.markingKey: (a) 'discrimination' means the behavioural component of prejudice, shown as unfair treatment of members of a group.
options: The behavioural component of prejudice, shown as unfair treatment of members of a group
The tendency to act in a particular way towards the attitude object
The feature of an attitude that indicates how positive or negative it is
A group whose norms an individual accepts as a model for attitudes and behaviour

items.stem: Distinguish between prejudice and discrimination.
items.answer: Prejudice – negative attitude towards a group (cognitive and affective); discrimination – behaviour showing unfair treatment of the group; one can exist without the other.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: Prejudice – negative attitude towards a group (cognitive and affective); discrimination – behaviour showing unfair treatment of the group; one can exist without the other.

items.stem: "Intergroup contact can reduce prejudice." Examine this statement with reference to attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination.
items.answer: The statement is valid. It brings the groups together in a cooperative setting and corrects stereotypes.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: 1 for accepting or qualifying the statement, 1 for the reason (it brings the groups together in a cooperative setting and corrects stereotypes.), 1 for supporting evidence from the chapter.

items.stem: According to Zajonc, the presence of others produces:
items.answer: arousal that improves performance on well-learnt tasks
items.markingKey: (d) arousal that improves performance on well-learnt tasks.
options: obedience
social loafing in every task
conformity
arousal that improves performance on well-learnt tasks

items.stem: Distinguish between the fundamental attribution error and the actor-observer effect.
items.answer: FAE – overweighting internal causes for others' behaviour; actor-observer effect – we explain our own failures by external causes but others' failures by internal causes.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: FAE – overweighting internal causes for others' behaviour; actor-observer effect – we explain our own failures by external causes but others' failures by internal causes.

items.stem: Give a reason for the following: First impressions are hard to change.
items.answer: The primacy effect gives more weight to information received first.

Read the following statements about social cognition; behaviour in the presence of others:

I only
II only

items.stem: Explain the process of attribution and the errors involved.
items.answer: Explaining causes of behaviour as internal (ability, effort) or external (task, luck); fundamental attribution error; actor-observer effect; Heider's distinction.

Study the extract below and answer the questions.

Impression formation and attribution are influenced by the perceiver, the target and the situation. Stereotypes are group-based schemas."

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes is correct?
items.answer: Beliefs are the cognitive component of attitudes and values contain a 'should' or 'ought' aspect.
items.markingKey: (c) The others are wrong: Valence tells whether the attitude is positive or negative. Attitudes are relatively stable. It has affective, cognitive and behavioural components.
options: Valence tells how central an attitude is.
Attitudes are momentary and change every day.
Beliefs are the cognitive component of attitudes and values contain a 'should' or 'ought' aspect.
An attitude has only an emotional component.

items.stem:
Read the following extract on social cognition; behaviour in the presence of others and answer the questions that follow.
"Some traits such as 'warm' and 'cold' are central traits that strongly affect the impression formed. Schemas function as mental short-cuts in social cognition. Stereotypes are group-based schemas."
(i) Assuming that a friendly person is also honest is an example of the: (1)
(ii) Explain the term 'social loafing' as it relates to this theme. (1)
(iii) Explain the reason behind the following: People often blame a stranger's failure on lack of ability. (2)
items.answer: (i) halo effect (ii) The reduction in individual effort when working in a group on a collective task. (iii) The fundamental attribution error gives more weight to internal factors for others' behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) halo effect (ii) The reduction in individual effort when working in a group on a collective task. (iii) The fundamental attribution error gives more weight to internal factors for others' behaviour.

items.stem: Which term describes the following? A small grain of reality that some stereotypes may contain, which leads people to hold on to them.
items.answer: kernel of truth
items.markingKey: (b) kernel of truth: a small grain of reality that some stereotypes may contain, which leads people to hold on to them.
options: social loafing
kernel of truth
primacy effect
social psychology

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A smoker who knows smoking causes cancer may stop smoking.
Reason (R): Prejudice can exist without discrimination and discrimination can exist without prejudice.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (b) Both statements are true, but R deals with a different point and does not explain A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Distinguish between 'schema' and 'prototype'.
items.answer: Schema: a mental structure that guides social cognition by organising information about objects, persons and events. Prototype: a concept-based schema defined by a set of features or properties that defines an object completely.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for explaining 'schema' (a mental structure that guides social cognition by organising information about objects, persons and events.) and 1 mark for 'prototype' (a concept-based schema defined by a set of features or properties that defines an object completely.), with the contrast between them made clear.

items.stem:
Read the following statements about attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination:
I. Attitudes predict behaviour better when they are strong and occupy a central place in the attitude system.
II. Learning, a strong social identity with ingroup bias, scapegoating, kernel of truth and self-fulfilling prophecy are sources of prejudice.
III. Prejudice and discrimination are the same thing.
Which of these statements are correct?
items.answer: I and II only
items.markingKey: (d) I is correct. II is correct. III is incorrect: Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is the behaviour.
options: II and III only
I and III only
I only
I and II only

items.stem: In the study of explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes, the term 'valence' refers to:
items.answer: The feature of an attitude that tells whether it is positive or negative towards the attitude object
items.markingKey: (d) 'valence' means the feature of an attitude that tells whether it is positive or negative towards the attitude object.
options: A negative attitude towards a particular group, often based on stereotypes
The feature of an attitude that indicates how positive or negative it is
The tendency for information presented first to have a stronger effect on impression formation
The feature of an attitude that tells whether it is positive or negative towards the attitude object

items.stem: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
items.answer: S.M. Mohsin – two-step concept
items.markingKey: (b) S.M. Mohsin – two-step concept. Solomon Asch – conformity and impression formation; Leon Festinger – cognitive dissonance; Fritz Heider – balance theory are the correct pairs for the others.
options: Leon Festinger – balance theory
S.M. Mohsin – two-step concept
Solomon Asch – cognitive dissonance
Fritz Heider – conformity and impression formation

items.stem: Read the case and answer. Children who admire a film star first identify with him, and when he starts promoting tree planting, they begin planting trees too. Name the theory of attitude change shown here and explain it briefly.
items.answer: Mohsin's two-step concept: the target first identifies with the source; when the source changes, the target imitates the change.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming it (Mohsin's two-step concept); 1 mark for the explanation (the target first identifies with the source; when the source changes, the target imitates the change).

items.stem: The following statement about attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and justify your correction: "Prejudice and discrimination are the same thing."
items.answer: Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is the behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement (Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is the behaviour.); 1 mark for a supporting fact from the NCERT chapter.

items.stem:
Read the following extract on explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes and answer the questions that follow.
"The four features of attitudes are valence, extremeness, simplicity or complexity, and centrality. Attitudes have affective, cognitive and behavioural components. An attitude system may include several related attitudes about one object."
(i) The three components of attitude are known as the: (1)
(ii) Explain the term 'affective component' as it relates to this theme. (1)
(iii) Explain the reason behind the following: Attitudes are evaluative. (2)
items.answer: (i) A-B-C components (ii) The emotional aspect of an attitude, such as liking or disliking the attitude object. (iii) They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) A-B-C components (ii) The emotional aspect of an attitude, such as liking or disliking the attitude object. (iii) They carry a positive or negative view of the attitude object.

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about social cognition; behaviour in the presence of others is correct?
items.answer: Impression formation and attribution are influenced by the perceiver, the target and the situation.
items.markingKey: (a) The others are wrong: It overweights internal causes when explaining others' behaviour. That is the recency effect; primacy refers to information presented first. Performance on well-learnt tasks improves; on new or difficult tasks it may worsen.
options: Impression formation and attribution are influenced by the perceiver, the target and the situation.
The fundamental attribution error overweights external causes.
Social facilitation means people always perform worse in the presence of others.
The primacy effect means the last information has the strongest effect.

items.stem:
Statement: First impressions are hard to change.
Which one of the following best explains this statement?
items.answer: The primacy effect gives more weight to information received first.
items.markingKey: (a) The primacy effect gives more weight to information received first.
options: The primacy effect gives more weight to information received first.
The presence of others produces arousal that improves performance on a well-learnt task.
A highly credible source makes the message more convincing to the target.
The fundamental attribution error gives more weight to internal factors for others' behaviour.

items.stem: What is meant by 'self-fulfilling prophecy' in the context of attitude-behaviour relationship; prejudice and discrimination?
items.answer: The process in which a group that is the target of prejudice comes to behave in ways that confirm the prejudice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: self-fulfilling prophecy correctly explained as the process in which a group that is the target of prejudice comes to behave in ways that confirm the prejudice.

items.stem: Give a reason for the following: Members of a group may confirm the prejudice about them.
items.answer: The self-fulfilling prophecy makes them behave as others expect.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: The self-fulfilling prophecy makes them behave as others expect. (1 mark for the reason, 1 for linking it to the statement).

items.stem: The following statement about explaining social behaviour; nature and components of attitudes is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and justify your correction: "An attitude has only an emotional component."
items.answer: It has affective, cognitive and behavioural components.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement (It has affective, cognitive and behavioural components.); 1 mark for a supporting fact from the NCERT chapter.

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"In Mohsin's two-step concept, the target first identifies with the source and the source then shows attitude change. Attitudes are learnt through association, reward and punishment, modelling, group norms and exposure to information. Family, school, reference groups, personal experiences and the media are factors in attitude formation. Characteristics of the existing attitude, the source and the message, and the target all affect attitude change."
(i) Explain the term 'balance theory', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: A smoker who knows smoking causes cancer may stop smoking. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "Balance theory was given by Leon Festinger." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) Fritz Heider's theory that attitudes change when the P-O-X triangle of a person, another person and an object is unbalanced. (ii) The two cognitions are dissonant and the person reduces dissonance by changing one of them. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: It was given by Fritz Heider; Festinger gave cognitive dissonance.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) Fritz Heider's theory that attitudes change when the P-O-X triangle of a person, another person and an object is unbalanced. (ii) The two cognitions are dissonant and the person reduces dissonance by changing one of them. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: It was given by Fritz Heider; Festinger gave cognitive dissonance.

items.stem:
Read the following statements about attitude formation and change:
I. Attitudes are inherited and cannot be learnt.
II. Characteristics of the existing attitude, the source and the message, and the target all affect attitude change.
III. In Heider's theory, balance exists when the P-O-X triangle has three positive sides or two negative and one positive side.
Which of these statements are correct?
items.answer: II and III only
items.markingKey: (d) I is incorrect: Attitudes are learnt through experience, association, modelling and group norms. II is correct. III is correct.
options: III only
I only
All of them
II and III only

items.answer: II only

II only
Both I and II
Neither I nor II
